You don't have to give us their names but, rather, tell us whether you know how many accused there were, and were they locals from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Sarajevo, I know that Kujundzic was the only accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also telling us about watching through at the disco club window and that you observed exercises going on in the nearby building?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the same document, page 6 in the English version, and in B/C/S the number is 0645-4357. I apologise, Your Honours, it slipped my mind that we are now on P82. Can we go back to 0645 -- ET 0645-4352. That's the document I'd like the Court to produce again. Page 6 in the English version, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor asked you about the Percin disco club, the question was this: "What can you tell us about the facility, the Percin Disco?" Your answer was: "There were no windows, it was a run down disco club without much going on there." So what is true? Did you actually have a window to look through, or is it true that that disco club did not have any windows as a building?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you ever saw that facility or not. It has small --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you what is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may finish his answer first, and then we can see whether there is any need to put further questions. About the windows or no windows, could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two small windows with dimmed window panes, and you couldn't actually see much through those windows. There was also a door, it was a glass door through which you could see something, and that's the door that was our inlet of air. And through that door with glass panes, you could see people doing exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm going to finish talking about this document with the following question. My learned friend from Defence asked you on page 0645-4373 in B/C/S -- and I believe that in the English version it is page 22, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The Defence counsel asked you or, rather, faced you with your statement provided to the ministry where you stated that from the beginning of the war you were under house arrest, and after the actual arrest, you were in the camp, and then on the 12th of July, 1992, you were taken out to serve as a human shield and then you escaped, so you did not have an opportunity to see and listen what individuals were doing in Doboj. You only had some sporadic information about that. You confirmed that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then you stated to the Defence counsel's question who said, Very well, okay, whatever you said subsequently to the Court, whatever you heard, you only heard subsequently. And you confirmed and said yes. What I'm saying is that all that you heard from other people subsequently after you fled?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What subsequent information are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to put my question in the following way: The presiding judge asked you about White Eagles, and you said you never saw them.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question at first, but now I can tell you that I heard that only later --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a moment, just a moment, I will lead you. You said that you never saw the white --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, although I do not oppose now and then to interrupt a witness if he moves away from the question, we have not reached that point so the witness may first finish his answer. You said that you didn't understand the question at first, but now you can tell that you heard that only later. Did you want to add anything to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here when I said house arrest, it meant that I was allowed, not only me, but all of Doboj, that is all the population of Muslim or Croatian ethnicity were allowed to be away from home for three hours from 8.00 until 11.00. And for the remainder of the time we were not allowed to leave our homes. That is meant by house arrest. And during those three hours we were all able to see what was happening in Doboj because we went shopping, if that is what you wanted to hear when you asked your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, but let me now remind you of your statement and that is P83, where you said that after you were released for the first time by the local police officer, you stayed at home to guard your property because there were many thefts?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So what is correct, did you stay at home to guard your property, or did you go out from 8.00 until 11.00?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to go out to buy food to survive. How could I do that, because I didn't have any provisions at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But apart from that time, you sat at home and guarded your property?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the rest of the time, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The presiding judge asked you about the White Eagles. I now ask you whether you ever saw Seselj's men at Doboj?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard accounts of their presence. I said as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you ever seen Knindzes in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some men when there was the attack on Doboj when we were taken out to be a human shield. Well, they may have been Knindzes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the Arkan's men, you said that they wore red berets. If you had never seen them, how did you know that they were sporting red berets? Is that the result of information somebody else gave you later?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at Doboj they were considered to be Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But a minute ago you said you had never seen Arkan's men, now I'm asking you if you have never seen Arkan's men, how did you know how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the people when we met each other and I heard accounts of them being Arkan's men, people with red berets, camouflaged in military uniforms, and that they were Arkan's men, whether they were or they weren't, I don't know, because there were many soldiers, a great many soldiers in Doboj. I don't know who was who.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I only have two or three short questions left for you. Have you heard of Mico's group in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was that group composed of locals?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did they also sport red berets?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard of a group called SOS, which stands for Serbian Protection Forces, from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right. Just a last general question for you. At the beginning of your statement and at the beginning of your testimony here you said that it was shocking for you in Doboj that there were SDS rallies attended by Radovan Karadzic who visited Doboj. So let me ask you, whether there were any rallies of SDA in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Alija Izetbegovic come there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How often were they rallies of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of any parties, and I didn't go to those rallies, so I don't know. But I know that the SDP party had rallies and the SDS --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But I'm asking about the SDA.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly there were rallies of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Hoffmann, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just for a couple of brief questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, I just have a few questions for clarifications to you. In cross-examination today on page 4 [sic] of today's transcript you were asked about the Muslim police officers that you came across when you escaped from the human shield incident. My question to you is, those Muslim police officers that you talk about were from the Doboj SJB, were those at the time actually working in Doboj, that is in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Muslim police officers were all laid off, and there was a police station at Matuzici, and that's where they were to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: On page 20 of today's transcript, you were asked about, or it was suggested to you that paramilitary units came under the command of Stankovic. My question is to you, if you have any personal knowledge if the person that you did describe as Crnogorac, if you have any personal knowledge that he was personally under the command of Milan Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Further on today at page 23 you were asked about Predrag Kujundzic, and I think you have given answers to the extent that he was a leader of the Red Berets, at the same time you refer to him as a leader of Predrag's wolves. Can you please clarify as far as you know to what unit he belonged, as far as you can tell.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predo Kujundzic had his autonomous unit, and he was its leader, and it was composed of his fellow villagers. I know very little about him. I know that there was the unit, but I do know that he took us out to be a human shield, and I heard accounts of terrible misdeeds of his elsewhere. So they were an autonomous unit, but to what they belonged ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, you refer to page 4 of today's transcript. That was before the witness arrived. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Then that must be a misspelling in the transcript. I was referring to page 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: For the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it's my recollection that I heard you say 4, so before -- but let's not try to see who made the mistake, but let's be happy with the correction. Page 14 you were referring to. Fine, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And I would ask that we quickly look again at your previous statement which is now D5. Exhibit D5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if we can go to the page 13 in English, which I'm looking at the second last paragraph of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I think in B/C/S we have to go back one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, D5 is not yet in evidence. That is the result of a bit unclear procedure. D4 was tendered and was admitted. At the beginning of the questioning of the witness on a document, Mr. Jordash asked already that a number be assigned to it, that was D5, and then I said D4 is admitted into evidence, this document referring to D5, let's see what happens, and then you tender it if it makes sense to do so. Does it make sense, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: As a result of my cross-examination I would submit no, because such a small amount was referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which there were several references to the content of that document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There were several.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you read them all, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I read the bits that I questioned the witness on. I certainly took the view at the time that the evidence that the witness gave stood on its own without a need for the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there are two ways. Either you would like to have it in evidence, Mr. Hoffmann, and in those circumstances we'll either invite Mr. Jordash to tender it anyhow, or the number would be vacated, or that you tender it, that's another possibility. I leave it in your hands for the time being, and we'll check whether there's any good reason to have D5 in evidence despite what you just said, Mr. Jordash. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: My position would certainly be that it should be tendered into evidence, because there were several references made and not always, as far as I recall them, again I haven't checked now every single reference, but I think there were references made without always just quoting, and I think for the context it should well be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, in order to avoid confusion it would be very convenient if you would tender it, because then we would not have to understand or reference to D5 being reference, really, to a Prosecution exhibit. So it would be very practical if you would do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I clarify one issue, Your Honour, if it's tendered, is the whole document then evidence, or simply the bits we referred to during questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole document would be evidence. At the same time of course we would focus on the matters raised, because it would be, I would say, unfair both to the tendering party and to the witness to just take for the truth of the content everything else that we find in such a document. So I would say limited purposes. And if there would be any other striking matter in the air, that Chamber would expect at least one of the parties to draw the attention to that, and not just start seeking to find anything which the parties have not even addressed, unless it's very striking matter, but then it would be appropriate for the Chamber to bring that to the attention of the parties as well, so that they could consider either to ask the witness to be recalled or whatever. But the parties should be aware that if they use a document, that it is most practical in almost all circumstances that we have that document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I apply to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D5. Then, Mr. Hoffmann, no objections, I take it. No objections from Mr. Bakrac. Under those circumstances, D5 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I'm certainly not opposed to admitting this document, but this may be a convenient moment since Mr. Petrovic and I are new to this case, in order to avoid possible misunderstandings in the future, whether the documents of the first Defence counsel will be marked 1D and the documents tendered by us 2D, so as to avoid confusion once we start submitting documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is a practice which was developed in some cases. In other cases it was not. We'll consider the matter. Sometimes the difference is found in the number of the document on the 65 ter list. For example, a 1D, a 2D, or a 3D document means that that is a document uploaded by the first defendant, the second defendant, or the third defendant. We'll consider it, and we'll also consult with the Registrar on this matter, and then we'll finally settle this issue. Not necessarily to be done at this very moment. Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, briefly in this last paragraph of your statement, can you confirm that you did say in this statement to the Prosecutor's Office of the state court: "I did not know anything about the conduct of Predrag Kujundzic and his wolves." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if I can take you back to page 10 of Exhibit D5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Page 10 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: It's a rather long paragraph where mentioning is of Kujundzic and Blaskovic. I'm not quite sure right now of the B/C/S page. Before the first mentioning of Kujundzic, do you see that it says in your statement, and this is referring to the human shield incident on 12 July 1992: "The orders were issued by the soldier with the scar." Before then it continues with: "Next to the Praga, I saw Predrag Kujundzic ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us again who you refer to as the soldier with the scar?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to Crnogorac, also known as Golub as he was called by others. It's one in the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with this exhibit, and I have just one last question today. At the end of the cross-examination you were asked about the Mice group, that's at page 53 of today's transcript, and you said that you heard about them. Do I understand from that answer that you have not actually seen the Mice group?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico's group was established once I had escaped to the Federation, but I learned from -- about them from the papers, et cetera. I never saw them. I heard that the group consisted of Doboj citizens and that they had committed atrocities in the surrounding areas, Teslic and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since any after -- has the redirect examination triggered any need for further cross? Not. Then Mr. Hadzovic, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you very much for having answered to the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you escort the witness out of the courtroom. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness? Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then, Mr. Usher, you are invited to escort the next witness into the courtroom. No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the information we received. We are talking about witness C-1166.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there are no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just remind the court we are at 3 hours, maybe the Court could re-assess the situation of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I primarily focused on two sessions of one hour and 15 minutes. Mr. Stanisic, the next witness is about to arrive in court. We could take a --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STANISIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- break. But let me see, we -- if we are talking about three hours, we are talking about hours including Mr. Knoops, three hours, I understood three hours to be three hours of time in court that -- but let's ask Mr. Stanisic, because a normal court session goes from quarter past 2 until 7.00, which is four hours and 45 minute, on average 45 minutes breaks, a little bit more in this case, which then means that four hours remain. So whether we are talking about a net three hours or gross three hours is still to be considered. Mr. -- yes, one second only. Mr. Stanisic, we can do a few things. We can either take the full five quarters of an hour for this second session, which would mean approximately another ten minutes. You arrived a bit earlier than expected. We also could take a break now and then continue, but if you say I'd rather limit it to three hours today, then we'll adjourn for the day after the next ten minutes. Another way of proceeding is to take a bit of a longer break and then to spend another, well, let's say, another hour in court. I would like to know what you prefer. And let me be clear on one matter, it's important for this Chamber that we keep clearly in mind the medical reports we received. It is also important for this Chamber to carefully listen to what you tell us about your ability to focus on the proceedings. When expressing this, I think you should also keep in mind that short sessions may well result in more days in court finally if we would spend two hours instead of three hours in court, that might result being in court for a considerable higher number of days. So I would like to hear from you, having referred to medical reports, referred to what we'd like to hear from you, and what you certainly will be aware will be the result of this assessment, whether you would say, well, let's go on for another 10 or perhaps 15 minutes and then stop for the day, or whether you would say let's take a bit of a longer break and then spend still some more time, that would be anything between 50, 55 minutes. Could I hear from you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STANISIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the first time, Your Honours, I have an opportunity to speak about my health condition which is seriously impaired, and has been for the last ten years or so. For the first day, I have been able to leave my cell after seven months. I understand you and I wish to assist the Trial Chamber to work as efficiently as possible. However, I was just going to ask you for a break and a bit of rest because I'm indeed not feeling too good. And that is why, if I may be of some assistance to you, I would like to ask you to take a break now and then continue for the next 50 minutes or so after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your preference is that we would have a break now, that would be a break of, well, let's say, half an hour, and that we would then continue to hear the evidence of the next witness for another 50 minutes. You think you can cope with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STANISIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I know that it is in the interest of my co-accused in these proceedings for these proceedings to be as efficient as possible, and that's why I'm trying very hard to try and be of as much assistance as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, the Chamber appreciates your cooperative attitude. We'll have a break. We'll resume at 10 minutes past 6.00, and then we'll after that adjourn for the day at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I already asked the usher to escort the next witness into the courtroom, and it's you who is going to take the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. President. Good evening, Your Honours. Adam Weber on behalf of the Prosecution. The Prosecution at this time calls Marko Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and as I understand, he is on his way. Mr. Weber, there is a chance since one of the judges should leave at 10 minutes to 7.00, that you would have only half an hour at this moment because 10 minutes for 15 bis takes more time perhaps and that's a bit overdone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I can break whenever it's convenient for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Miljanic. Mr. Miljanic, first of all, you are already at the door and we couldn't continue at that moment, apologies for that. Before you give evidence the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you by Mr. Usher, and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help me God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution, and he is seated to your right over there. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good evening, sir, could you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I will kindly ask the interpreter to speak up because I'm a bit hard of hearing, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the volume be adjusted. Mr. Miljanic, if you would have any further problem, please tell us. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. My name is Marko Miljanic, I was born on the 12th of October, 1951, in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The official records of this Tribunal include evidence that you provided in the case of Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic; case number IT-02-54 on the 14th of July, 2003; transcript pages 24315, line 24, to page 24364, line 23. And in the case of Prosecutor versus Milan Martic; case number IT-95-11; on the 29th and 30th of March, 2006; transcript pages 2859, line 15, to page 2931, 15. Sir, do you recall giving evidence in the Milosevic and Martic cases on those dates?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to listen to your testimony from both the Milosevic and Martic cases?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now that you've taken the solemn declaration in this case, do you affirm the accuracy of the evidence you gave in the Milosevic and Martic cases?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you were to be asked the same questions here today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders the prior testimony of Marko Miljanic in the cases of Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic and Prosecutor versus Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could numbers be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The testimony from the Milosevic trial, 65 ter 5177, then becomes Exhibit P95. The testimony from the Martic trial, 65 ter 5178, and that becomes Exhibit P96.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you provide a signed statement to representatives of the ICTY on 26th of July, 1996?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As part of your testimony in the case of the Prosecutor versus Milosevic, did you review your 1996 ICTY statement and provide an addendum to your statement dated the 19th of June, 2003?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to review your 1996 ICTY statement and the 2003 addendum prior to your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 4 of the English version and page 3 of the B/C/S version of Prosecution 65 ter 5175. I believe we have the B/C/S versions of the document up on both screens. If I could please have the page 4 of the English version on one of the screens. In the B/C/S version could we please have the last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to the last paragraph on the B/C/S page before you of your 1996 ICTY statement, which is paragraph 4 from the top in the English version, is the date indicated at the beginning of this paragraph the correct date?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if you can see, the last paragraph which begins: "On 18th November 1996 ..." in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: There's a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is the correct date that should be stated in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With that correction, do you affirm the accuracy of the evidence you gave in your 1996 ICTY statement and the addendum of the 19th of June, 2003?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions here today, would you provide the same evidence that you provided in the statement and addendum?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution tenders the 1996 ICTY statement, which is 65 ter 5175, and the 2003 addendum which is 5176 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, those documents would receive numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those become Exhibit P97 and Exhibit P98, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, any objections against admission of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour. As to the documents of 2003, Defence observes it's not signed the by the witness, the English version is not signed by the witness. We have no objection to the tendering of the documents of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think as a matter of fact the signature is required under Rule 92 bis, but not under Rule 92 ter and since --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The B/C/S version is attested to and signed by the witness. It was done pursuant to the 92 bis procedure in the Milosevic case. It has been attested to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but again admission is now sought under Rule 92 ter, isn't it? I'm looking at the -- Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P95, P96, P97, and P98 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 2863, lines 10 through 14 of your testimony in the Martic case, you stated: "I have to say, that the entire population of Skabrnja on the 2nd of October, 1991, after heavy bombing, had been all moved out of the village. That's to say, all the population was moved out. The elderly people, women, and children. The only persons left in the village were men of a younger age." Sir, my question is, who was committing the heavy bombing prior to the 2nd of October, 1991, in Skabrnja and it's surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The JNA. The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was there any bombing on the 2nd of October, 1991, near the village of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where was this bombing occurring?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Across the entire village. The village of Skabrnja is 7 kilometres long from one end to the other, and not only Skabrnja, but also the other villages in the neighbourhood were shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What type of weapons were being used during these bombardments?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe the Prosecution could first ask whether the witness is competent to answer this question, the foundation to ask the witness who is not an expert as to the type of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but the answer is -- the question is not necessarily requiring expert knowledge, although, it could appear from the answer that there's reason to further explore the knowledge of the witness which allows him to answer the question. Let's first listen to the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, what type of weapons were being used during these bombardments?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I'm a former JNA officer. I knew exactly what weapons were used. Those were artillery weapons, mortars and aviation. Everything possible was used. All the weapons which existed at the time were used, save for the navy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before continuing with the next question, just for counsel's reference and Chamber's reference, this witness's experience is extensively discussed on page 2883 of Exhibit, now, P96.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What type of weapons were being used by planes during these bombardments?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Cluster bombs. On that day, as far as I can remember, four cluster bombs were dropped. Those kinds of bombs are banned by the Geneva Conventions, and there were also messages on the casings of those cluster bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, may I invite you to, as you do, answer the questions, but to limit your answers to what is asked. For example, Mr. Weber did not ask you whether cluster bombs were banned by the Geneva Convention. If he wants to know that, or if he, perhaps, doesn't already. Mr. Weber at the same time I'd like you to invite you to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- very carefully just referring to the special knowledge and even if that would amount to expert knowledge, of course the witness appears as a witness of fact, and therefore we should primarily focus on facts. If, for example, the witness says that artillery weapons, then of course that is a qualification. He mentioned mortars, whether he intended to say that it was mortars and other artillery weapons, mortars are often considered to be artillery weapons. We should really, since he is not introduced as an expert witness, wherever we come close to answers which require at least above average knowledge of certain matters, that you explore the factual basis for the answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What were the messages that were being dropped on the village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: For example, "greetings from the JNA for Tudjman's rats." Those were the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how many individuals stayed behind in the village of Skabrnja after the 2nd of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: About 250 people stayed on permanently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who were these individuals?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: They were members of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 24341, line 23 through page 24342, line 4, of Exhibit P97, you stated: "It wasn't actually a unit of any kind. And I said at the beginning that we created the structure on the basis of the civilian defence that existed in the former Yugoslavia, and civil defence had the task of preventing fires, elemental disasters, wars to defend the population, find shelter if there was a natural disaster, so that was the task in aim of what -- what we were now calling and referring to as a unit." Is this an accurate description of the responsibilities of the individuals who stayed behind in the village of Skabrnja after the 2nd of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What were the professions of the individuals who served in the local civilian defence to Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: They all had the civilian jobs. All of them but me. I was the only one who was MUP employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What types of jobs did these individuals have, if you could give us some examples?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: For example, the commander of one company was an auto mechanic. The commander of another company, which was another JNA formation, was an electrician. There were waiters, bricklayers, electricians, blue-collar workers, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Aside from yourself, were there any individuals that were members of the civilian defence that actually had military experience?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were the individuals that you describe as part of the civilian defence in Skabrnja an active or reserve duty?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: They were not members of any active formation. They were members of the reserve police, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 2868, lines 3 through 14 of Exhibit P96, you stated: "On the 5th, The Hague truce was signed. That's to say, on the 5th of November, 1991, when I was invited to come to Mr. Ivan Brzoja, chief of the police administration, who gave me a written and verbal order to the effect that The Hague truce was signed and that we ought not to provoke. I replied to this by telling him, Chief, we have nothing to provoke with. Can we really provoke the air force with the rifles that we have? He told me, I'm going to hold you responsible for this. You are a member of the police administration. I went about my business and things went back to normal, people resumed their jobs" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are reading, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. "I went about my business and things went back to normal. People resumed their jobs in the factory. However, the following day, on the 6th or, rather, on the following day, on the 6th, people were taken back to Skabrnja on five buses and life resumed as per normal."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people returned to Skabrnja on the 6th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: About 300 people on buses and an additional number in their own cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you stated "we have nothing to provoke with" what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: We simply didn't have weapons to be able to provoke, and we had no ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What type of weapons did the civilian defence have?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember now, we had about six machine-guns, 7.9 millimetres; a so-called Sorac [phoen], the German type. There were two mortars with four shells; and 30 to 40 per cent, I'm not sure, of hunter's rifles or sport rifles, or trophy armament from the Second World War. And some half automatic rifles or assault rifles, some 20 to 30 in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After the 6th of November 1991, you stated that things went back to normal and people resumed their jobs. Did the members of the civilian defence in Skabrnja also return to their regular jobs?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was the cease-fire maintained until the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please describe any military movements that you observed between the 6th and 17th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: There was very little military movement in that period. I personally saw Ratko Mladic passing. Only him and tanker trucks from the Zemunik airfield in the direction of Benkovac and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where did you observe these military movements?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: On the road above Skabrnja. That's the road from Benkovac to Zemunik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know what military these vehicles were a part of?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was there anything impeding the movement of these JNA vehicles between the 6th and the 17th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Nobody impeded them. They could move freely. Both them and civilian vehicles, they all could pass freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to go into the events of the 18th of November, 1991, would Your Honours like me to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have some six minutes left, if you can deal with a portion in the next six minutes, then you can start. If you think it's impossible to make any sense out of the next six minutes, then we'll stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd be happy to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the 18th of November, 1991, on page 2869, lines 5 through 9 of Exhibit P96, you stated: "On that morning, I was sleeping in a house in the centre of the village by the radio set we had. It was this ordinary police radio set. The lad who was seated by the radio set, I asked him whether there was anything new to report. He told me, No, Marko, there's nothing new." At approximately what time did this conversation occur?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Around 7.00 a.m., possibly a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who were you receiving reports from at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Around Skabrnja at Razovljeva Glavica, that's a hill above Skabrnja, I had about 10 people in a reconnaissance group, and they informed me of everything, because from that hill you could see all of Skabrnja and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have the ability to communicate with anywhere else besides this reconnaissance group?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, or, rather, yes, but only through messengers. And at that place I also had a field telephone set.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time were any members of the civilian defence on duty in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I can't give an exact number but around 100 in the whole village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where were these members of the civilian defence stationed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: In the whole village, I remind you that the village is 7 kilometres long, and they were stationed throughout the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 2869, lines 9 through 19 of Exhibit P96, you stated: "At about 7.30 tanks could be heard from the direction of Benkovac. At that point since I had people at Razovljeva Glavica, which is an elevation above Skabrnja standing guard, one of the men there informed me over the field telephone line that the tanks were arriving, also from the direction of Gornje Zemunik, the airport there. I had three couriers of mine and I sent them to inform the civilians to flee to their shelters and to take their positions above the village. At that point, that was about 7.30, I don't recall the exact time, fierce artillery fire was opened upon the village from tanks and artillery pieces. The entire village was ablaze." Who opened fire on the village with tanks and artillery?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The JNA did. Whether there was anybody else with them, but certainly the JNA because they all these types of armaments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where is Gornje Zemunik located in relation to Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: To the north-west of Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how far?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: 600 to 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is the distance between Razovljeva Glavica and the centre of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: About 200 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to mobilise all 240 plus members of the civilian defence in Skabrnja prior to the commencement of this tank and artillery attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I'm looking at the clock. If it would be one or two questions, fine, but if it would be more, then I would invite you to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I may ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did the three couriers have the opportunity to inform the civilians to flee to their shelters prior to the JNA forces attacking Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: They did prior to, before, the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: During the attack, once the attack had started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, my question was whether or not the couriers had the ability to inform the civilians before the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, but once the attack had started, then they were sent out to inform the people, once they started shelling the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, then, that they were not informed beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I can break there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Due to an extraordinary schedule, Mr. Miljanic, we'll resume only next week. I don't know how this is arranged. I take it that the witness will stay over, but I'm not fully informed about that. But we will continue to hear your evidence only in one week from now, that is on the 8th of December in the same courtroom in the afternoon. Any other matter to be raised before we ... Then, Mr. Miljanic, I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that's testimony you have given already today or testimony which is in the statement or in the transcripts of the other cases, or whether it's about testimony still to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Starting next week. We adjourn, and we'll resume on Tuesday, the 8th of December, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of December, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.54 p.m.,
